The evidence explicitly states that these methods 'provide better image quality' (visual fidelity) but come 'at the cost of significantly higher computational cost and memory bandwidth.' The evidence also notes that the choice depends on application requirements, implying they are chosen when quality is the priority. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.

Strengths: Higher image quality, especially at large magnification factors, avoiding the artifacts associated with trilinear interpolation [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that higher order interpolation methods provide higher image quality, especially at large magnification factors, and avoid artifacts associated with trilinear interpolation. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states that 'higher order interpolation methods such as cubic convolution or B-spline interpolation' achieve 'better quality' than trilinear. It also notes that trilinear interpolation causes 'three dimensional diamond structures or crosses' (artifacts) when using 'large magnification factors'. Therefore, all facts in the claim are present in the evidence.

- Aliasing: Interpolation of scalar values is prone to aliasing if high-frequency details are missed by the classification step, regardless of the interpolation order [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that interpolation of scalar values is prone to aliasing if high-frequency details are missed by the classification step, regardless of the interpolation order. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Interpolation of scalar values is usually prone to aliasing since depending on the classification used, high frequency details might be missed.' While the evidence does not explicitly use the phrase 'regardless of the interpolation order' in that specific sentence, the context of the document discusses various interpolation methods (nearest neighbor, trilinear, cubic, B-spline) and notes that the aliasing issue is inherent to the scalar interpolation process dependent on classification, rather than being a flaw specific to one order. The core fact—that scalar interpolation is prone to aliasing due to missed high-frequency details during classification—is directly supported. The 'regardless of order' aspect is consistent with the general statement about scalar interpolation being 'usually prone to aliasing' in the context of the described techniques.
